newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Crude in Asia at 13-month low, economies benefit.
newsitem.headline: Crude in Asia at 13-month low, economies benefit.

text.p: Crude oil prices in Asia have slumped to their lowest level in a year, largely as the result of pressures in Europe and the United States.

High refinery runs, rising stock levels and weak demand in the United States along with ample Brent North Sea crude supplies have pressured the key oil futures markets in London and New York, traders said.
The prompt July Brent futures contract in London fell to $17.45 per barrel on Tuesday -- the lowest level since May 20, 1996.
The same contract, which trades on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX), traded as low as $17.50 on Wednesday before rising slightly to $17.58.
Analysts said the decline in prices, which extends a slide that started in January, would benefit most Asian economies.
Brent peaked in October at $25.06 per barrel -- its highest level since the Gulf War.
While it held just under those levels for the last quarter of the year, the price has fallen 30 percent since.
Other crudes have followed suit, easing import bills around Asia and leaving budget projections for buying crude in surplus.
Asia guzzles around 18 million barrels of crude oil each day, but produces only 7.3 million barrels per day, leaving the rest to be made up by imports.
Some countries, like Malaysia and Indonesia are net exporters. So they benefited last year when prices rose to five-year highs, but were unlikely to benefit now, the analysts said.
"India stands out on the benefit side," said James Brown, a regional oil analyst for Merrill Lynch. "They will be breathing a sigh of relief."
"They were facing a massive blow out on the oil pool deficit because they are a massive importer," he said, referring to India's fuel subsidy system.
India produces around 600,000 bpd of crude, but imports an equal amount.

India's oil pool deficit system, which covers the gap between high international prices and low subsidised domestic prices, ran up a deficit of 155 billion rupees in the financial year ended March 31 because of the high prices last year.

The government is bracing itself to bite the bullet and raise domestic prices to start cutting back the subsidy deficit. The last time prices were raised, in 1996, there was a huge political and public outcry.
Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral has promised a final decision on raising prices this weekend.
Analysts said the slide in prices this year had allowed the Indian government to delay the decision, but a rise in its domestic prices was still needed.
But importers could be experiencing a relatively low price for 1997, analysts said. Average prices are expected to be higher.
Brown said Merrill Lynch forecast an average Brent prices in 1997 of $18.05 and $19.05 in 1998.
NYMEX futures, which fell to a 16-month low of $18.55 on Tuesday, were expected to average $19.50 in 1997 and $20.50 in 1998, Brown said.
These compared with an average Brent price in 1996 of $20.05 and average NYMEX prices of $22.14.
-- Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3081)
